# Check hull fairness in Rhino

::: {.lesson-meta}
**Exercise 6 · About 30 minutes · Complete Exercise 2 first**

Use a curvature graph and Zebra stripes to inspect a hull, then see how one control-point change affects a curve.
:::

## Before you start

Open the finished `surname_ex02_hull.3dm` from [Exercise 2](02-hull-modelling.qmd) and save a copy as `surname_ex06_fairness.3dm`. Keep the original hull unchanged. Turn on the `20_rails` and `30_hull` layers so the `sheer` rail and hull are visible.

## 1. Read a curvature graph

Select the `sheer` rail and run `_CurvatureGraph`. The short lines, or hairs, show how the curve bends. Change the graph display scale if the hairs are difficult to see. A sudden jump or spike is a clue to inspect; the graph is a guide, not a pass/fail score.

Read McNeel's illustrated examples of [curvature graphs](https://docs.mcneel.com/rhino/8/help/en-us/commands/curvature.htm) and its [boat-hull fairness guide](https://docs.mcneel.com/rhino/mac/usersguide/en-us/html/ch-16_boathull.htm). The hull guide shows a sheer curve and explains why fewer, well-placed control points are usually easier to fair.

Run `_CurvatureGraphOff` before continuing.

## 2. See what a control-point move does

Make a copy of the `sheer` rail with `_Copy`. Use `w0,0,0` as the base point and `w10,0,0` as the destination, placing the copy clear of the hull. Select the copied curve, run `_CurvatureGraph`, and turn on its control points with `_PointsOn` (F10 on Windows).

In the **Front** view, select one interior control point and move it about **0.05 m upward in world Z** with the Gumball. Watch the curve and graph change. Take a screenshot, then use Undo to restore the copied curve. Confirm that its graph returns to its earlier shape, then hide the control points and graph. Do not edit the original `sheer` rail.

## 3. Inspect the hull with Zebra

Select the hull and run `_Zebra`. Rotate the view to inspect the reflections along the hull and across the centreline join. Look for stripes that kink, jump or change abruptly. See McNeel's [illustrated Zebra examples](https://docs.mcneel.com/rhino/8/help/en-us/commands/zebra.htm), which compare stripe behavior at different surface connections.

The Zebra display helps reveal surface smoothness. It does not check dimensions, topology or whether the hull is watertight.

## Submit

Submit `surname_ex06_fairness.3dm` and two screenshots:

1. The copied `sheer` rail with its control points and curvature graph, showing the effect of the temporary move.
2. The hull with Zebra stripes visible at the centreline join.

In two or three sentences, describe what changed in the curvature graph when you moved the point and what you observed in the hull's Zebra stripes.

**Reference library:** [Rhino analysis references and visual examples](../resources.qmd#rhino-analysis-and-fairness-examples).
